rpm_packages_teaching.prerequisite_note: Before this task: Find a project and prepare its handover. Read the three concepts below before using the different gallery example.

concepts.title: Installed records and supplied archives
concepts.text: rpm -q NAME reads an installed record. rpm -qp /absolute/file.rpm reads an available local package header without installing it. NAME means the header package name; PATH in archive commands means a supplied absolute archive path. In the read-only inspector, choose Available local archives to find those paths. A filename is not proof of its package name. -ql lists recorded paths and -qpl lists a local archive manifest.

concepts.title: A requirement names a capability
concepts.text: rpm -q --requires NAME shows the consumer's declared requirements. rpm -qp --provides PATH shows what a local package can provide. A package's own name is one capability, but another package name may provide the needed versioned API. >= means the capability version must be at least the displayed version. A high package version with only an unversioned provide does not satisfy a versioned requirement.

concepts.title: Choose explicitly, then check the current result
concepts.text: rpm -i PATH installs absent names from the supplied local archives; it does not download or solve dependencies. Multiple paths form one explicit logical set. This simulation requires the resulting whole installed database to be healthy, an extra restriction rather than a universal RPM transaction rule. Unmodeled or refused forms show a simulator explanation without an invented RPM failure number. rpm -e NAME erases the named installed package; at the end retain the stated records/files.

rpm_packages_teaching.prerequisite_note: Before this task: Find a provider beyond its package name. Read the three concepts below before using the different print example.

concepts.title: Version has three parts
concepts.text: RPM compares epoch, then version, then release. An omitted epoch means zero. Epoch 1 with version 1.0 can be newer than epoch 0 with version 99.0. This is RPM ordering, not semantic version ordering; arbitrary letter-by-letter or decimal ordering is unsafe.

concepts.title: Read epoch explicitly
concepts.text: Default rpm -q output is name-version-release.arch and hides epoch. To display it, use rpm -q --queryformat '%{NAME}\t%{EPOCHNUM}:%{VERSION}-%{RELEASE}.%{ARCH}\n' NAME. NAME is the installed package; each %{...} selects that header field and EPOCHNUM prints numeric epoch, including zero. Single quotes keep the format literal; its backslash-t and backslash-n produce a tab and newline. With the same format, -qp and a supplied archive path inspect a local candidate. Other formats are outside this subset.

concepts.title: Upgrade a coherent explicit set
concepts.text: rpm -U PATH may install an absent name or replace a same-architecture record with a strictly newer version. It is not an exact-reinstall or downgrade option. Give the consumer and needed provider paths together, or update a compatible provider first. Configuration contents/manifests are unchanged here; modified-config sidecars are not modeled.

rpm_packages_teaching.prerequisite_note: Before this task: Update a client when epoch changes the order. Read the three concepts below before using the different garden example.

concepts.title: Recorded ownership can outlive a file
concepts.text: rpm -ql NAME lists its recorded manifest even when a current virtual file is missing. rpm -q --path PATH finds recorded ownership of an absolute virtual file path, including a missing file. rpm -qf PATH is admitted only for an existing owned regular virtual file; on a missing path this subset gives a simulator explanation, not a claimed real RPM error code.

concepts.title: Compare virtual payload separately
concepts.text: The optional inspector compares declared header payload with actual simulated file bytes and attributes. A package record alone does not prove those files match. This is explicitly not rpm -V, a signature check or evidence that software runs.

concepts.title: Repair the recorded version
concepts.text: rpm --reinstall PATH uses the exact currently recorded local archive. It restores ordinary virtual payload files. Here the configuration is unchanged and must remain so; modified/missing configuration or changed configuration manifests require deferred behavior and are refused. rpm -U would change the installed version and is not this exact repair.

rpm_packages_teaching.prerequisite_note: Before this task: Repair recorded payload without upgrading it. Read the three concepts below before using the different hall example.

concepts.title: Find actual installed providers
concepts.text: rpm -q --whatprovides CAPABILITY lists installed providers, not candidates in local files. rpm -q --provides NAME reads an installed provider's capabilities; rpm -qp --provides PATH reads a local candidate. Compare these with the consumer's rpm -q --requires NAME requirement. The header package name and provided capability can differ.

concepts.title: Stage the handover before erase
concepts.text: Install an eligible alternative explicitly with rpm -i PATH, then erase the old package with rpm -e NAME. Erasing the only needed provider is refused by this logical whole-database-health rule, without pretending to produce universal real-RPM failure output.

concepts.title: Preserve outcomes, not a method badge
concepts.text: At completion the consumer must still be installed with its initial record/files, all its requirements satisfied, the retired provider absent and the neighboring package retained. Other coherent explicit command sets that reach these outcomes are valid. No action history, resolver, package execution or service availability is assessed.
